def: An open-source inference engine that serves many generate requests at once on one or more GPUs, with a paged KV cache and continuous batching.
A Python library for running one program across a cluster: a driver starts actors and tasks on any node and calls them through futures.
The tool that builds container images and runs containers from them, through a background service (the Docker daemon) on each node.
A cluster manager that keeps declared pods running on a fleet of machines and restarts what dies.
The batch scheduler of most supercomputer-style clusters: a job waits until all its nodes are free, then starts on all of them at once.
A long-lived process with state, such as an engine or a trainer rank, called through futures.
A Ray reservation of several bundles, each a set of resources that must fit on one node (such as 8 GPUs and 64 CPUs), placed together (PACK) or apart (SPREAD), all or nothing.
Ray's way of passing GPU tensors between actors directly over NCCL or NIXL, with only a reference going through Ray.
PyTorch's collective library for CPU tensors, used beside NCCL, for example by asynchronous checkpoints.
Start a job only when every pod or rank can run; also called gang scheduling.
A frozen filesystem with code and libraries, built in layers; a container is a running instance of one, an ordinary process sharing the host kernel.
A process's request to the operating-system kernel, such as opening a file or a socket; gVisor intercepts them, runc lets them reach the host kernel.
In Linux, a container's private view of files, processes or the network; in Kubernetes, a team's folder of objects with its own permissions.
Outbound network traffic; sandboxes block it except to an internal package mirror.
vLLM's scheduler-and-cache process, which runs one engine step (one forward pass over the batch) at a time; a block table lists the 16-token cache blocks that hold one request.
A recording of an engine step's GPU kernel launches, replayed in one call; it holds fixed memory addresses, so new weights are copied in place.
Sharing GPU memory between processes on one machine through handles; how colocated engines read the trainer's weights.
vLLM freeing its GPU memory for a colocated trainer: level 1 moves the weights to CPU memory and drops the cache, level 2 drops both.
Making the trainer use the experts the engine's MoE router chose for each token, so both compute the same function.
Kubernetes' unit: one or more containers scheduled together on a node.

An add-on that teaches Kubernetes a new kind of object and keeps it running, such as KubeRay (Ray clusters), JobSet (a group of pods run as one job, which Kueue admits as a gang) or LeaderWorkerSet (multi-node inference replicas).
Kubernetes job queueing: quotas per ClusterQueue, borrowing within a cohort, priorities, preemption.
NVIDIA's collective library (all-reduce, broadcast, all-gather) over NVLink and the network.
One machine's network card (NIC) reading or writing another machine's memory directly, without either CPU; InfiniBand (a dedicated cluster network) and RoCE (RDMA over Ethernet) carry it.
NVIDIA's library for moving tensors directly between GPUs, across machines over RDMA; used for KV-cache transfer and weight sync.
PyTorch's n-dimensional grid of ranks with named dimensions, such as replicate, shard and tp.
A tensor that knows how it is split or replicated across a DeviceMesh; FSDP2 parameters are DTensors.
fully_shard: shard parameters, gradients and optimizer state across data-parallel ranks, gathering one block at a time.
Hybrid sharding: shard within a group of GPUs, replicate across groups, all-reduce gradient shards between them.
PyTorch Distributed Checkpoint: each rank saves its shards in parallel; loads reshard to a new layout.
Tensor, expert, pipeline and context parallelism; Field Guide §2 covers each.
Mean time between failures; for a job, the per-GPU value divided by the number of GPUs.
The checkpoint interval √(2 × blocking time × MTBF) that minimizes expected lost time.
Items in a system = arrival rate × time each spends there.
Time to first token; time per output token after it.
Requests per second that meet every latency target. The Field Guide also uses it for RL: tokens that reach the loss per GPU-hour, the inverse of §10's GPU-hours per useful token.
Reusing the KV cache of a shared prefix (a system prompt, earlier turns) instead of recomputing it.
Running prefill and decode on separate pools and moving the KV cache between them.
Moving cache blocks to host memory or disk so they survive eviction from GPU memory.
Exchanging token IDs with the engine instead of text, so nothing is re-tokenized.
A counter bumped on every sync; the orchestrator attaches it to every generated token span.
A sample removed from training because the infrastructure failed, as distinct from a reward of zero.

Taking whichever groups have finished from a small window at the head of the submission-ordered queue (completion order inside the window, input order behind it), so batches don't skew toward short trajectories.
The low-variance KL estimator r − 1 − log r, where r is the trainer-to-engine probability ratio of a sampled token; used here to compare the two on the same tokens.
Sandboxes started ahead of demand so a trajectory doesn't wait for start-up.
Container runtimes for the same images: runc, Docker's default, runs on the shared host kernel; gVisor answers system calls in a user-space kernel; Firecracker gives each sandbox its own small VM.
A full stage making its upstream wait, instead of letting work pile up.
A request ID that makes retries safe: the second attempt returns the first result.
A change applied to a small part of the fleet first, or a fixed probe whose result must not change; canary log-probs are the Field Guide's parity probe.
